# Thin Bidding: The Cheapest Attention Is Wherever Nobody Else Is Buying.

Source: https://lowob.com/research/thin-bidding/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-04-30 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Distribution

> Summary: Ask a media buyer why a click costs what it costs and you will hear about audiences, creative and relevance scores. All of that is true, and none of it is the first cause. The first cause is the number of companies bidding for the same person's attention at the same moment. Where the crowd is thick, attention is expensive; where it is thin, attention is cheap, whether or not anyone has noticed. WARC estimates Alphabet, Amazon and Meta took 56.1% of global ad spend outside China in 2025. Look where few look, and measure before you commit.

## Key points

- Every ad auction, creator rate card and affiliate payout table is a price set by crowding.
- WARC forecasts the three largest platforms' share of global ad spend outside China rising from 56.1% in 2025 to 58.0% in 2026.
- Meta's average price per ad rose 14% year on year in Q3 2026, faster than its 10% rise in impressions.
- Bidding thins where a channel is unglamorous, inconvenient or closed to a category by platform policy.
- Thin is not the same as cheap: the cheapest open-exchange inventory is often cheap because nobody real is there.

That is the whole idea behind how we choose channels, and it is simple enough to put in one sentence: look where few look.

## Why the crowd gathers in the same place

Companies buy where the buying is easy. The large platforms made a specific bet: give any company with a credit card a self-serve interface, an audience of billions and instant reporting, and the bidding will take care of itself. It did. The convenience is real, and so is the price it produces.

The concentration is measurable. WARC's December 2025 forecast put Alphabet, Amazon and Meta at 56.1% of global advertising spend outside China in 2025, about $556.6 billion, rising to 58.0% in 2026 and 58.8% in 2027. WARC expected the three to absorb the vast majority of incremental ad spend over that period. When most new money goes to the same few auctions, the same few auctions get more crowded.

The price follows. Meta reported that in the third quarter of 2026 its ad impressions rose 10% year on year while the average price per ad rose 14%. Price per ad also reflects ad performance, format and geographic mix, so the figure is not a pure measure of crowding. But price rising faster than supply is also what a crowded auction looks like from the outside.

The result is a market in which most marketing budgets compete in the same three or four auctions, against the same well-funded companies, for the same scroll. In that market, the buyer with the largest budget or the most patient investors wins, and everyone else pays a premium to be visible for a moment.

## Where the bidding thins out

Bidding thins for three reasons, and only one of them is that a channel is bad.

| Why bidding thins | Typical channels | What it asks of the buyer | How to read it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The channel is unglamorous | Affiliate programmes, comparison sites, maintained email lists, niche newsletters, mid-sized creators with buying audiences | Patience with small volumes and plain reporting | Cost per outcome in your own systems |
| The channel is inconvenient | Anything that requires recruiting people rather than uploading a file, or six weeks to stand up rather than six minutes | Operational work most competitors will not do | Outcome per hour of setup, as well as per dollar |
| The platforms said no to the category | Affiliate and creator networks, programmatic inventory and publishers that carry restricted categories | Compliance work and a claims library | Delivery and outcome by source, against the platform you cannot use |

**The channel is unglamorous.** None of the first row makes a good slide. All of it is priced accordingly.

**The channel is inconvenient.** It reports in spreadsheets rather than dashboards. Inconvenience is a form of thin bidding, because most companies will not do the work.

**The platforms said no to the category.** This is the one that matters most to the companies we work with. Google Ads, for example, requires certification for crypto exchanges and software wallets, approves them only in listed countries, and prohibits initial coin offerings and DeFi trading protocols outright. Roku's Ads Manager requires prior approval for any crypto ad, limits approvals to the US, and bans ads for individual securities. When a platform restricts a category, the well-funded competitors who would otherwise crowd the open channels are stuck in the same review queue. The affiliate networks, creator networks and programmatic inventory that carry those categories are thinly bid, not because they do not work, but because the platforms that would have made them unnecessary said no. Our piece on [distribution when ad platforms restrict you](https://lowob.com/research/distribution-when-ad-platforms-restrict-you/) maps that open band in more detail.

> The channels your category can actually use are usually the ones your competitors have written off, which is precisely why they are worth measuring first.

## Thin is not the same as cheap

There is a trap in the idea, and it is worth naming. The cheapest inventory in advertising is the open programmatic exchange, and much of it is cheap for a reason. The ANA's 2023 study found made-for-advertising sites, pages built to host ads and filled with bought traffic, took about 21% of impressions and 15% of spend in its sample. That inventory is not thinly bid attention. It is barely attention at all.

Thin bidding means a real audience that few competitors are paying to reach. A personal-finance newsletter with, say, 40,000 engaged readers and three sponsors is thinly bid. A page of scraped content with twelve ad slots is cheap. The test that separates them is the same in both cases: did anything happen that your own systems can see? Our pieces on [programmatic numbers you can trust](https://lowob.com/research/programmatic-media-numbers-you-can-trust/) and [ad fraud](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ad-fraud/) cover how to tell a low price from a low-value impression.

## The discipline that makes it work

Cheap attention is only valuable if you can tell whether it did anything. Thin bidding without measurement is just a smaller invoice.

So the method has two halves that have to be held together. Measure cheaply, in several places at once, before committing anything. Then, when a channel reads, put everything behind it. Companies that only do the first half end up with a portfolio of half-run experiments. Companies that only do the second half are back in the crowded auction, having skipped the part where they found out.

| Half | What it means | Common failure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Measure cheaply, in several places | Small, simultaneous tests with tracking the company controls and a decision written in advance | Tests too small to read, or measured on clicks |
| Commit when a channel reads | Move budget decisively to the channel with the best cost per outcome | Spreading budget evenly to avoid choosing |

Thin channels make the first half harder, because volumes are small. Our piece on [campaign testing that reaches a decision](https://lowob.com/research/campaign-testing-that-reaches-a-decision/) sets out the sample sizes a test needs at B2B volumes, and [demand generation economics](https://lowob.com/research/demand-generation-economics/) shows how to set a cost-per-outcome ceiling before the first dollar goes out, so a channel that reads can be scaled without a second debate.

## What this looks like in practice

The answer is not always the obscure channel. Sometimes the crowded auction is worth its price. The point is that the decision is made on a measurement rather than on convenience.

Illustrative example: letting the measurement choose

Decision
:   Before consolidating spend onto the largest platform, run a one-week measurement across the three channels competitors were ignoring, with tracking the company controlled.

Reason and owner
:   A noisy fintech company was spending across six channels and could not say which one produced a customer. The instinct was to consolidate onto the platform with the best reporting. Owned by the growth lead.

What changed
:   Two of the three ignored channels produced nothing readable. One niche publisher produced funded accounts at a lower cost than the main platform and was scaled. The main platform stayed in the mix, now judged on the same outcome.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size consumer fintech, built from patterns across engagements.

The price of attention is a crowding effect. The channels your category can actually use are usually the ones your competitors have written off, which is precisely why they are worth measuring first.

## lowob takeaways

- **Price is crowding.** The number of bidders sets the cost of attention before creative or targeting do.
- **The crowd is concentrated.** Three platforms take most global ad spend and most of its growth.
- **Thin channels are unglamorous, inconvenient or closed to rivals.** All three can be opportunities.
- **Thin is not cheap.** Low-priced inventory with no real audience is waste, not opportunity.
- **Measure, then commit.** Small tests in several places, then decisive budget behind the one that reads.

## Common questions

### Why are online ads getting more expensive?

Mostly because more advertisers bid for the same audiences in the same few auctions. WARC estimates Alphabet, Amazon and Meta took 56.1% of global ad spend outside China in 2025, and Meta's average price per ad rose 14% year on year in Q3 2026.

### What are underpriced marketing channels?

Channels where few competitors bid: affiliate programmes, comparison sites, niche newsletters, mid-sized creators and, for restricted categories, publishers and networks the large platforms do not replace. Each has to be measured on outcomes before it is scaled.

### Where can crypto and fintech companies advertise if platforms restrict them?

Often through affiliate and creator networks, programmatic inventory and publishers that accept the category, subject to their own policies. Google and Roku, for example, allow some crypto advertising only with certification or prior approval, and only in listed markets.

### Is cheap inventory the same as an underpriced channel?

No. Much cheap programmatic inventory sits on made-for-advertising sites with no real audience. An underpriced channel has a real audience that few competitors are paying to reach.
